extractions.source_title: Anthracnose of Banana | Plantix Library - Pests & Diseases

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Anthracnose is caused by the fungus Colletotrichum musae

affected_parts.evidence: Dark-brown to black, sunken spots on fruit. Develops to larger patches.

summary.value: Dark-brown to black sunken spots on banana fruit peel that coalesce into larger black patches, with orange to salmon pink fungal growth in their center, leading to premature ripening and rotting.
summary.evidence: Dark-brown to black, sunken spots on fruit. Develops to larger patches. Orange to salmon pink colored fungal growth in their center. Premature ripening and rotting.

diagnostic_features.value: Dark-brown to black lenticular sunken lesions with pale margins on green fruit peel; on yellowing fruits, variable-sized lesions coalescing into sizable black sunken patches with orange to salmon pink colored fungal growth in their center; symptoms can start at the tip of the fruit from former floral infection.
diagnostic_features.evidence: Initial symptoms are visible on green fruits, and are characterized by dark-brown to black lenticular, sunken lesions with pale margins on the peel. On yellowing fruits, these lesions are of variable sizes and can coalesce to become sizable black sunken patches. Orange to salmon pink colored fungal growth appear in their center. The symptoms can also start to appear on the tip of the fruit and result from a former floral infection.

extractions.source_title: Banana bunchy top (121) - Pacific Pests, Pathogens & Weeds Fact Sheet

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Scientific Name Banana bunchy top nanavirus.

type_of_disease.evidence: BBT is caused by a virus.

affected_parts.evidence: Plants with banana bunchy top (BBT) have narrow, progressively shorter leaves with little distance between them, hence the name 'bunchy top'. Plants that are infected when young rarely produce a fruit bunch. When diseased suckers are planted they become severely stunted and they do not produce fruit.

summary.value: Plants show narrow, progressively shorter leaves clustered together giving a 'bunchy top' appearance, with upward-rolling leaf edges and yellow margins. Dark-green dots and dashes appear along minor leaf veins in a 'Morse-code' pattern, with hooks curving downwards near the midrib.
summary.evidence: Plants with banana bunchy top (BBT) have narrow, progressively shorter leaves with little distance between them, hence the name 'bunchy top'. Leaf edges often roll upwards with yellow margins. The most characteristic symptoms are short, dark-green dots and dashes along the minor leaf veins, so-called 'Morse-code' patterns, which form hooks curving downwards near the edge of the midrib

diagnostic_features.value: Short, dark-green dots and dashes along the minor leaf veins forming 'Morse-code' patterns, with hooks curving downwards near the edge of the midrib. Leaves are upright, stunted, and cluster in the throat of the plant ('choked').
diagnostic_features.evidence: The most characteristic symptoms are short, dark-green dots and dashes along the minor leaf veins, so-called 'Morse-code' patterns, which form hooks curving downwards near the edge of the midrib. Notice the leaves are upright, stunted and tend to cluster in the throat of the plant; leaves like this are said to be 'choked', and give the bunchy top symptom.

disease_name.evidence: Common name of the disease Fusarium wilt

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Causal agent Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense

type_of_disease.evidence: a lethal fungal disease caused by the soil-borne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense

affected_parts.evidence: The fungus enters the plant through the roots and colonizes the xylem vessels thereby blocking the flow of water and nutrients. Disease progression results in the collapse of leaves at the petiole, the splitting of the pseudostem base and eventually plant death.

summary.value: Vascular wilt disease causing internal vascular discolouration ranging from pale yellow to dark red or black, external wilting and yellowing of older leaves, leaf collapse at the petiole, and splitting of the pseudostem base, eventually killing the plant.
summary.evidence: Fusarium wilt is a typical vascular wilt disease. The fungus invades the vascular tissue through the roots causing discolouration and wilting, eventually killing the plant.

diagnostic_features.value: Characteristic internal vascular discolouration varying from pale yellow in early stages to dark red or almost black in later stages. Yellowing and wilting progresses from older to younger leaves. Collapsed leaves hang down the pseudostem like a skirt. Splitting of the base of the pseudostem. Vascular discoloration is peripheral in the pseudostem. Fruit does not show any specific disease symptoms.
diagnostic_features.evidence: The characteristic internal symptom of Fusarium wilt is vascular discolouration, which varies from pale yellow in the early stages to dark red or almost black in later stages. Externally, the first signs of disease are usually wilting and yellowing of the older leaves around the margins. The collapsed leaves hang down the pseudostem like a skirt. Splitting of the base of the pseudostem is another common symptom. The fruit does not show any specific disease symptoms.

look_alikes.evidence: The leaf symptoms of Fusarium wilt can be confused with those of the bacterial disease Xanthomonas wilt. In countries with Moko disease, which is caused by Ralstonia solanacearum race 2, and also causes vascular discoloration, it is possible to confuse the two diseases.
